case_study_insert.main_stem: Frostmere Cold Chain (FCC) is a partnership between Sofia and Marco Benedetti in the cold-storage logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2012, the business stores and distributes frozen food for supermarkets and food manufacturers across the Breymore region, using a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership from Sofia as managing partner. FCC plans to invest $780,000 in a new automated sub-zero depot with robotic picking, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 from the partners' capital. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.25 a unit and a selling price of $18.75, and produces 70,000 units a year (each unit being one pallet handled). FCC faces labour turnover of 26% among its forklift operators and two recent safety incidents.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Temperature Report — Q3 2026: The depot handled 17,300 pallets last quarter with temperature compliance of 98.6%, down from 99.4% in June after a refrigeration fault. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. Energy use was 41,000 kWh for the quarter. A survey of 120 supermarket and manufacturer clients found that 74% would renew contracts if temperature compliance stayed above 99%, and 63% rank automated picking as the key factor in renewals. Labour turnover among forklift operators is 26%. Off-site forklift recertification costs $520 per operator.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Frostmere Cold Chain for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, increasing repayments on variable-rate overdrafts and loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $11.40 to $12.10 per hour from April 2027, lifting depot wage bills. (3) Commercial electricity and refrigerant costs have risen 16.8% year-on-year, while frozen food demand grew 4.2% and cold-chain diesel costs rose 7.4%.

questions.question_text: FCC plans to finance its $780,000 depot expansion partly with $300,000 from the partners' capital. Explain two advantages for FCC of using partners' capital to fund the expansion instead of the $480,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Partners' capital carries no interest and no repayment schedule, which protects FCC's thin 32%–36% margins and its cash flow while the automated sub-zero depot is commissioned. The business already pays interest payable that rose from $30,000 to $36,000 in 2025, and adding $480,000 of bank debt would deepen that further; funding $300,000 of the cost internally keeps the partnership's distributions and working capital intact.

Point 2: Using their own capital shows commitment and discipline — both partners have their personal wealth tied to the depot's success, which reassures the 120 surveyed clients whose renewals depend on 99% temperature compliance, and strengthens FCC's position if further finance is needed later from the bank or from asset-backed leasing. Unlike a bank loan, no collateral is pledged against the existing cold stores, and the partners avoid covenant risk while robotic picking is bedded in and the 26% forklift-operator turnover is being fixed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FCC's financing, expansion and thin margins.

questions.question_text: FCC is promoting its new automated sub-zero depot capacity to supermarket chains and food manufacturers. Consider advertising in food industry trade magazines, telemarketing to the 120 surveyed clients, or hosting an open-house launch event at the new depot. Which should FCC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Food trade magazine advertising: Trade titles reach food manufacturers and retail buyers nationally and would publicise the sub-zero depot and robotic picking to a broad audience at moderate cost. However, national circulation wastes spend on firms outside the Breymore region, the message cannot demonstrate the 98.6% temperature compliance that 74% of clients demand as a renewal condition, and ROI is hard to track against contract wins.

Telemarketing to the 120 surveyed clients: Direct calls convert research into contracts efficiently — FCC knows 74% want 99% compliance and 63% rank automated picking first, so a scripted offer of compliance reports and site visits is timely and measurable. But cold calls can irritate senior cold-chain managers, reach only one contact per firm, and a phone pitch cannot prove depot capability, so conversion depends heavily on follow-up visits.

Open-house launch event at the depot: An invitation-only open evening lets all 120 decision-makers walk the sub-zero aisles, watch robotic picking, handle compliance data and meet Sofia Benedetti — the strongest possible proof of the 74% renewal criterion and the 63% automation priority. Cost per head is modest, press coverage is likely, and the event itself is memorable. Limitation: capacity is limited, attendance is not guaranteed, and one poorly run evening would damage relationships.

Recommendation: FCC should choose the open-house launch event, followed by telemarketing follow-ups within two weeks. Live demonstration is the only channel that proves automated picking and 99% compliance to all 120 clients at once, and it maximises renewal probability before competitors respond. Trade magazine advertising is rejected as too broad and unverifiable for a regional partnership; telemarketing alone is rejected as a weak substitute for proof, though it is essential for chasing signatories after the event.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to FCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of FCC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FCC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and telemarketing alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: FCC has labour turnover of 26% among forklift operators and two recent safety incidents. Explain two benefits for FCC of introducing team working for its forklift and picking crews.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working gives forklift operators and pickers shared responsibility for each shift, building peer monitoring of loads, speeds and refrigeration-handling rules. Crews look out for one another near the racking and in sub-zero aisles, reducing the kind of near-miss behaviour behind the two recent safety incidents and reinforcing safe practice faster and more credibly than top-down autocratic orders from the managing partner, whose distance from the freezer floor makes direct supervision patchy.

Point 2: Working in stable teams deepens knowledge of stock rotation and temperature-critical handling, improving pick accuracy and cutting the rework that drives customer complaints and the 98.6% compliance slip from June's 99.4% benchmark. Teams also give operators variety and social contact in an isolated cold environment, easing the strain of monotonous freezer work and directly attacking the 26% labour turnover among forklift operators, which in turn cuts recertification costs of $520 per operator and keeps certified cover on every shift around the clock.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FCC's turnover, safety and compliance.

questions.question_text: FCC must improve forklift safety and cut operator turnover of 26%. Consider on-the-job safety coaching paired with a near-miss reporting bonus, or off-the-job recertification at $520 per operator with refresher courses. Which should FCC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job safety coaching plus near-miss bonus: Coaching on live shifts gives immediate, job-specific feedback on racking speeds, load handling and refrigerant zones, while the bonus rewards every verified near-miss report — creating pride in prevention rather than fear. It is cheap per head, keeps all 50 staff productive during the $780,000 depot commissioning, and directly targets the two recent safety incidents. Limitations: bonuses can distort reporting (people invent near-misses or hide real ones to keep payments), and coaching depends on the skill of the supervisor under an autocratic managing partner who may undermine open reporting.

Off-the-job recertification at $520 per operator: Formal recertification at $520 per operator resets baseline competence, provides audit-ready certificates for supermarket client inspections, and removes operators from riskier live coaching scenarios. It is ideal for new recruits replacing the 26% turnover outflow. Limitations: operators leave the floor for training (reducing capacity during depot launch), generic content may not match FCC's specific sub-zero racking and robot interfaces, and it does not by itself change day-to-day behaviour between refresher courses.

Decision: FCC should choose on-the-job safety coaching with a near-miss reporting bonus as the primary measure, with recertification reserved for new starters. It is faster, cheaper and builds a reporting culture for the two recent incidents; at $520 per operator, full recertification for every picker would cost $26,000 for 50 staff, a poor trade while turnover — not competence — is the deeper problem. Pure off-the-job recertification is rejected as the main fix because generic certificates expire behaviourally and remove operators during commissioning; layering recertification only on recruits keeps cost contained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to FCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of FCC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of FCC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, behaviour and compliance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FCC's management can use its cost, break-even and handling data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 70,000 − ($315,000 ÷ ($18.75 − $11.25)) = 70,000 − 42,000 = 28,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 28,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.75 − $11.25 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FCC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. FCC can compare the 42,000-unit break-even output with 70,000 pallets handled, confirming a 28,000-unit margin of safety so the $780,000 depot expansion is comfortably covered before the partners commit further capital.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.50 lets Sofia Benedetti test renewal pricing for the 74% of clients demanding 99% temperature compliance, for example whether a service-level premium still covers the $315,000 fixed costs and $480,000 bank loan.
3. Managers can stress-test the 16.8% rise in electricity and refrigerant costs, since colder storage feeds the $11.25 variable cost directly and cuts the $7.50 contribution, prompting early renegotiation of client tariffs.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost — fixed cost per unit of $315,000 ÷ 70,000 = $4.50 plus the $11.25 variable cost, giving $15.75 a unit — to spot waste in energy and racking, renegotiate supermarket rates, and target which pallet contracts are genuinely profitable.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 28,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 28,000 units vs 70,000 pallets; renewal pricing for compliance clients; stress-testing the 16.8% electricity rise; and unit-cost benchmarking at $15.75 across contract types.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FCC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has FCC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 32.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 36.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 11.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 13.0%
ROCE 2024 = 11.0%
ROCE 2025 = 13.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,800,000 revenue − $1,224,000 cost of sales = $576,000, giving $576,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 32.0%; 2025 = ($2,100,000 − $1,344,000) = $756,000 ÷ $2,100,000 = 36.0%. After operating expenses: 2024 $198,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 11.0%; 2025 $273,000 ÷ $2,100,000 = 13.0%. Capital efficiency: 2024 $198,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 11.0%; 2025 $273,000 ÷ $2,100,000 = 13.0%.

Evaluation: Performance has improved, but from a thin base. The trading margin widened from 32.0% to 36.0% as automation and better client mix offset electricity inflation, and the operating margin rose from 11.0% to 13.0% despite interest payable increasing from $30,000 to $36,000 as the $480,000 bank loan was drawn. Capital efficiency improved from 11.0% to 13.0% as capital employed rose by $300,000 to $2,100,000, suggesting the depot plan is beginning to deliver returns. However, cost of sales still grew to $1,344,000 alongside the 16.8% electricity and refrigerant rise and 29-to-17 complaint progress is fragile; temperature compliance of 98.6% remains below the 99% renewal threshold for 74% of clients, so revenue could stall if the depot automation falters.

Conclusion: FCC's financial performance has improved. Trading margins rose from 32.0% to 36.0%, operating returns from 11.0% to 13.0% and capital efficiency from 11.0% to 13.0%, on revenue growth of $300,000. The partners should not get complacent: margins remain thin for a cold-chain operation and hostage to energy costs, so FCC should complete the depot commissioning smoothly, renegotiate electricity tariffs and convert the 74% willing clients into signed renewals before further expansion debt is added.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether FCC has improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FCC of automating the new sub-zero depot with robotic picking.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Robotic picking directly answers the 63% of clients who rank automation as the key renewal factor and is FCC's best chance of lifting temperature compliance back above the 99% threshold demanded by 74% of the 120 surveyed clients. Machines do not suffer cold-induced fatigue, pick accurately at depth and speed, and cut errors and damaged stock behind the falling complaints (29 to 17 per month), so FCC can credibly promise service levels that justify premium rates on renewed contracts.

Disadvantage: Automation is the riskiest part of the $780,000 depot investment — software faults, sensor drift or maintenance delays could idle the whole sub-zero line, breaching cold-chain compliance and triggering penalties and lost clients just when renewal talks peak. It also displaces some forklift and picking roles in a 50-strong, autocratically led partnership where two recent safety incidents have already strained morale, so redundancy or redeployment decisions must be handled transparently or turnover of the remaining 26% of forklift operators will deepen.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FCC's depot, clients and workforce.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.1% increase in the minimum wage to $12.10 and the 16.8% rise in commercial electricity and refrigerant costs will affect FCC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): A 0.5% rise on the $480,000 bank loan adds about $2,400 a year to financing costs, compounding the increase in interest payable from $30,000 to $36,000 already seen in 2025. It also lifts overdraft costs on variable-rate working capital ahead of the cold-chain peak season. Real but small, and largely avoidable by fixing the loan rate, this is the mildest of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $12.10 from April 2027): With 50 staff concentrated in forklift, picking and cleaning roles, the insert gives the new floor at $12.10 per hour, up $0.70 from $11.40, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.70 an hour and the depot wage bill rises broadly from April 2027. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely; partly offset by the frozen food demand growth of 4.2% and by the incentive structure around the 99% compliance target, the rise is material but can be absorbed if renewal pricing improves.

Electricity and refrigerant cost inflation (16.8%): Energy is the lifeblood of a cold-storage facility — the depot drew 41,000 kWh in one quarter and refrigeration runs continuously. A 16.8% rise feeds straight into the $11.25 variable cost of every pallet handled across 70,000 units a year. The insert does not split the variable cost by input, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — for illustration only, if the energy-linked portion were $1.00 per pallet, a 16.8% rise on it would add $0.168 per pallet, or about $11,760 a year across 70,000 pallets — illustrative only. Meanwhile diesel costs only rose 7.4%, so FCC's energy bill is inflating far faster than transport fuel, striking precisely the cost base behind its margins.

Conclusion: The 16.8% rise in commercial electricity and refrigerant costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes FCC's single most relentless operating cost, scales with every pallet handled (41,000 kWh drawn in one quarter and refrigeration that runs continuously), and directly threatens the margins already squeezed to 32%–36%. The wage rise is significant but manageable through compliance bonuses and price increases, and the interest-rate rise is small and fixable. FCC should secure fixed electricity tariffs, audit the new depot's refrigerant efficiency and pass energy surcharges into contract renewals immediately.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to FCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FCC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FCC with a well-justified judgement that electricity and refrigerant inflation has the greatest impact.
